y1: Seeing the faith of the friends, Jesus first said to the paralyzed man, 'Your sins are forgiven.' The teachers of the law thought to themselves, 'This is blasphemy.' Because only God can forgive sins.
y2: Jesus said, 'But that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins,' and made him walk. The visible healing proved the invisible forgiveness.
y3: The words 'Your sins are forgiven' cannot be verified, so they seem easy to say. But 'Get up and walk' is immediately verified. By doing what seemed harder, Jesus showed that He could also do what is truly hard.
y4: From the Tax Booth to the Table
y5: A tax collector was someone who collected taxes from his own people for Rome and Herod. He was considered a traitor and a fraud, and was shunned in the synagogue. The name of this Gospel is that very tax collector, Matthew.
y6: When the Pharisees asked, 'Why does He eat with tax collectors and sinners?', Jesus quoted Hosea 6:6: 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.'
y7: Mark and Luke call him 'Levi', but the Gospel of Matthew uses the name 'Matthew' and introduces him as 'Matthew the tax collector' in the list of disciples in 10:3. It is a confession that boasts of grace without hiding his past.
y9: Jesus compared Himself to a bridegroom and said that new wine must be put into new wineskins. The kingdom of heaven that Jesus brought cannot fit into old molds.
y10: A woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years was considered 'unclean' according to the Law and could not touch people. When she touched the fringe of Jesus's cloak, Jesus did not let her hide; He called her 'daughter' and restored her publicly.
y11: The stories of the woman who had been sick for twelve years and the twelve-year-old girl (Mark 5:42) are woven together. Both were associated with 'uncleanness' (blood, a dead body), but Jesus touched both and restored both as 'daughters'.
y13: Jesus raised the dead girl to life, and healed the blind and the mute. Chapters 8 and 9 end with the same sentence (9:35) as 4:23.
y14: When Jesus saw the crowds, He had compassion on them because they were 'harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.' 'The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into His harvest field.'
y15: 'Had compassion' (splanchnizomai) comes from the word for 'internal organs'. It is a sympathy so deep that you feel an ache in your gut. This heart leads to the sending out of the disciples in the next chapter (Chapter 10).
verse: 'Those who are healthy have no need for a physician, but those who are sick do. … For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.'
prayer: Jesus, thank You for being the Doctor who came to call not the righteous, but sinners. Let me not forget that I too am a called sinner, just like Matthew. Give me a heart that has compassion on my friends who are like sheep without a shepherd, and use me as a harvest worker. I pray in the name of Jesus Christ. Amen.
d0: paralytic. This is the root of the English word paralytic. Because he couldn't go to Jesus himself, he needed the help of his friends. The Gospel of Mark records that his friends dug through the roof (Mark 2:4).
d1: tax collector. He collected more than the required amount and kept his share. In Jewish society, he was considered a 'sinner' on the same level as prostitutes. Zacchaeus was also a chief tax collector (Luke 19).
d2: mercy. 'Hesed' in the book of Hosea is unchanging, faithful love. It means God desires love for people more than the form of worship. Jesus quotes this verse again in 12:7.
d3: have compassion. In the New Testament, this word is almost exclusively used for Jesus (and God in the parables). The father of the prodigal son also 'had compassion' and ran when he saw his son (Luke 15:20).
